around: Bangladesh, 3 other South Asian countries launch new initiative to tackle extreme heat | Prothom Alo Login Bangladesh International Sports Opinion Business Youth Entertainment Lifestyle Claim vs Fact Search ই-পেপার বাংলা Login Climate Bangladesh, 3 other South Asian countries launch new initiative to tackle extreme heat Staff Correspondent Dhaka Published: 08 Oct 2026, 15: 37 Four new country briefs assessing heatwave conditions, preparedness and gaps in Bangladesh, India, Nepal and Bhutan were released at the Global Heat Forum, which began in Bangkok, Thailand, today. Courtesy: GHHIN The El Niño phenomenon is strengthening across the Pacific, increasing the risk of another season of extreme heat in South Asia. Against this backdrop, India, Nepal, Bangladesh and Bhutan have launched a joint initiative to tackle the impacts of extreme heat. Four new country briefs assessing heatwave conditions, preparedness and gaps in the four countries were released today, Thursday, at the Global Heat Forum, which began in Bangkok, the capital of Thailand, says a press release. The briefs were published under the initiative of the South Asia Hub of the Global Heat Health Information Network (GHHIN). The assessments were conducted as part of a review of countries’ preparedness and capacity as health risks from extreme heat continue to rise across South Asia. They examine how the countries are responding to extreme heat, preparing in advance and where significant gaps remain. The Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW) in New Delhi runs the South Asia Hub. Its partners include the Sustainable Futures Collaborative, Natural Resources Defense Council, BRAC James P Grant School of Public Health, and the UN Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (UNESCAP). The initiative is also aligned with the joint climate and health programme of the World Health Organisation (WHO) and the World Meteorological Organization (WMO). Heatwaves in South Asia have become more intense and longer in recent years. Extreme heat causes more than discomfort; it poses serious health risks, particularly for children, older people, pregnant women and outdoor workers. In addition to heat-related illness and deaths, extreme heat can increase the risks of heart disease, respiratory illnesses and other health problems. The purpose of the new assessments of the four countries is to identify areas where progress has been made in addressing heat-related health risks and where more coordinated action is needed. The findings could be used in policymaking, strengthening health systems, early warning systems and protecting vulnerable populations. The Global Heat Forum in Bangkok is discussing the growing risk of extreme heat and its health impacts in South Asia and other regions around the world. Experts have warned that climate change could further increase the risk of heatwaves in the future. As a result, there is growing emphasis on treating heat not simply as a weather event but as a major public health risk. In Bangladesh, the feels-like temperature, which takes both temperature and humidity into account, has risen by about 4.5°C since 1980. People now spend nearly one-third of the year in dangerously humid heat. Heat has been recognised as a risk in Bangladesh’s National Adaptation Plan. The country’s first urban heatwave action plan has been developed for Narayanganj. National guidelines for dealing with heat-related illness and a public awareness campaign called “Beat the Heat” have also been launched. Despite these initiatives, however, there is a lack of dedicated heatwave action plans at both national and local levels. It is also important to establish a system for monitoring heat-related illness by linking weather forecasts with hospitals and the health system. These findings and recommendations are included in the first Bangladesh assessment by the South Asia Hub of the Global Heat Health Information Network (GHHIN). Four separate assessments of heat and health conditions in Bangladesh, India, Nepal and Bhutan were released today, Thursday, at the Global Heat Forum in Bangkok, Thailand. First assessments of the four countries This is the first assessment by the GHHIN South Asia Hub of heat and health risks in the four countries. At the time of the release, it was announced that El Niño is strengthening in the Pacific, which could increase the risk of another season of extreme heat in South Asia. Against this backdrop, Bangladesh, India, Nepal and Bhutan have begun working together to address the impacts of extreme heat. Plans have advanced, but implementation remains a challenge The assessment of the four countries says preparations for tackling heat in South Asia have progressed most rapidly in the areas of planning, weather forecasting and early warning. All four countries have developed heatwave action plans and early warning systems in one form or another. However, measures to translate these plans and warnings into protection on the ground have not advanced at the same pace. Major gaps remain in monitoring heat-related illness, financing local-level initiatives, and integrating heat risks into health, labour and urban planning. While several countries have begun large-scale initiatives, progress is uneven. Extreme heat was once mainly seen in the plains of South Asia. It is now spreading to the Himalayan countries of Nepal and Bhutan as well. Health risks in Bangladesh remain under-recognised Farzana Misha of the BRAC James P Grant School of Public Health said, “Heat is one of the least recognised health risks in this region. It is less visible than floods or cyclones. But its impacts on health, work and food security are no less serious. In Bangladesh, we have already started taking some initiatives. A national guideline for dealing with heat-related illness and the country’s first urban heatwave action plan in Narayanganj have been developed. Similar initiatives are being undertaken in Dhaka, Rajshahi and other urban centres. Now similar action is needed across South Asia. We need to build health systems and provide the necessary financing so that risks can be identified before the heat arrives and action can be taken before people are affected.” The Bangladesh assessment recommends developing dedicated heatwave action plans at both national and local levels. It also calls for establishing a system to monitor heat and health by linking the country’s weather forecasts with hospitals. India has made the most progress Among the four countries, India has made the most progress in shifting from reactive relief measures to anticipatory action to reduce heat risks. District-level research by CEEW found that 57 per cent of India’s districts are at high or very high risk of extreme heat. Nearly three-quarters of the country’s population live in these districts. More than 250 heatwave action plans are in place at the city and district levels in India. Heatwaves have also been officially recognised as a natural disaster under the country’s disaster risk management financing framework. A national system for monitoring heat-related illness has been established, and more than 18,000 medical officers have been trained. However, the assessment recommends taking India’s heat action plans beyond the boundaries of disaster management. It calls for dedicated financing and systems to assess health outcomes to be included in every plan. Nepal experienced 50 days of temperatures above 40°C Nepal, a Himalayan country, has traditionally faced floods, droughts and other water- and weather-related disasters. It is now also facing the risk of extreme heat. According to data from Nepal’s national meteorological department, temperatures in the country’s southern Terai plains exceeded 40°C for 50 days in 2024. Nepal has already published its first national heatwave action plan and issues risk-based warnings. However, the country’s health system does not yet routinely record data on heat-related illness. The assessment recommends making it mandatory for hospitals in the Terai region to record admissions related to extreme heat. It also calls for strengthening the process of ensuring that weather warnings reach local communities and that appropriate action is taken accordingly. Heat is rising even in Bhutan’s cooler valleys Bhutan’s southern lowlands are becoming warmer. As a result, temperatures are also rising in valleys that were previously cooler. Communities that had never before needed to plan for extreme heat are now at risk. Bhutan’s national policy assigns responsibility for tackling heat to the Ministry of Health. A 2022 regulation also requires measures to protect workers from heat. Bhutan has relatively advanced early warning systems for floods and glacial lake outburst disasters. The assessment says these systems could also be expanded to cover heat. It recommends bringing different policies and responsibilities together to develop an integrated national heatwave action plan. Forecasts must be turned into protection Biswas Chitale, a fellow at CEEW and chair of the GHHIN South Asia Hub, said extreme heat is now a year-round regional risk in South Asia. However, the region does not have to start from scratch in tackling the risk. Every country is projected to experience worse heat conditions than five years ago. According to Chitale, the key task now is to link weather forecasts with health systems, local budgets and labour regulations. A warning must be turned into effective protection for people. Kyeong Ko, director of the Information and Communication Technology and Disaster Risk Reduction Division at UNESCAP, said heat does not stop at borders. Therefore, responses to it should not be confined within national borders either. Countries can share forecasts, coordinate temperature thresholds for taking action and incorporate heat risks into existing disaster management systems. Following the Global Heat Forum, the South Asia Hub will develop a regional network and training programme involving various organisations. Situation assessments will also be prepared for the governments of the four countries before and after the heat season. The goal will be to turn scientific information on heat into coordinated action and ensure the protection of the region’s most vulnerable populations. This includes funding for targeted efforts in Indonesia and Thailand next year, alongside preparations for a second Southeast Asia Heat Health Forum. Tools, evidence and lessons from these efforts will be shared across the region to strengthen coordinated action on extreme heat. Established in January 2025 as GHHIN’s first regional hub, the Hub brings together governments and partners to strengthen collaboration, advance evidence and support action on extreme heat across Southeast Asia. GHHIN is a global network of policymakers, scientists and practitioners and an initiative of the World Meteorological Organization, World Health Organization (WHO) and US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The Hub is based at the Heat Resilience & Performance Centre (HRPC), Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, National University of Singapore (NUS Medicine), and draws on more than a decade of heat resilience research and the university’s role as a neutral platform for regional convening. PAA complements this as a catalytic

ng funder collaboratives and cross-sector partnerships that direct capital towards shared outcomes. Turning regional collaboration and data into country-led action Across Southeast Asia, action on extreme heat is growing but remains fragmented. While early warning systems and municipal heat action plans are expanding, many countries still lack a standing mechanism for robust coordination between health, labour, urban and disaster agencies. Data varies across countries and successful pilots often can lose their institutional footing once funding ends. Shaun Seow, Chief Executive Officer of the Philanthropy Asia Alliance, said: "Extreme heat sits at the intersection of climate, health and the economy, which is why responsibility for it can fall between institutions designed to address each area separately. The challenge is to connect the science with public agencies and local communities in ways that endure, so we can move from protecting hundreds of thousands of people to hundreds of millions." PAA’s support will build on the Hub’s regional foundation by advancing sustained, country-led action while strengthening the evidence and shared learning available across Southeast Asia. Advancing heat health action in Indonesia and Thailand In Indonesia, the Hub is building on the ongoing Project KATALIS-HEAT, delivered with WHO Asia-Pacific Centre for Environment and Health (ACE), WHO Indonesia, and the Ministry of Health. The work strengthens national coordination and advances city-level heat action in Makassar and two additional cities. Efforts in Thailand are at an earlier stage, with partner consultations and a rapid stocktake laying the groundwork for longer-term action and helping stakeholders to agree on shared priorities for the next phase of work. Lessons from both countries will flow back into the Hub’s regional platform, enabling governments elsewhere in Southeast Asia to build on tested approaches rather than start afresh. Sharing lessons across Southeast Asia Working alongside the governments, researchers, funders and implementation partners already active on heat,

Hub , said: "The Hub is designed so that progress in one country can help accelerate action in another. Evidence generated with governments can be adapted elsewhere, while frontline experience helps shape the questions researchers pursue. By bringing these insights together across Southeast Asia, we can build a stronger body of practical knowledge that countries can draw on and adapt to their own contexts. This next stage aims to build on the foundation we have and support governments in developing heat-health responses that are locally relevant and sustainable over the long term." About the Philanthropy Asia Alliance Philanthropy Asia Alliance (PAA) is a Temasek Trust initiative dedicated to catalysing collaborative philanthropy in Asia through dynamic multi-sector partnerships. By harnessing collective strengths, PAA multiplies impact, accelerates positive change, and takes urgent action to address the pressing environmental and social challenges of our time. PAA’s flagship programme is the annual Philanthropy Asia Summit. For more information, visit philanthropyasiaalliance.org. Share: The Thirst of a City - India GHHIN-EJN Extreme Heat Photo Contest 2025 - Ayanava Sil Related Topics Health At Mumbai Climate Week, the WMO-WHO Climate and Health Joint Programme, The Rockefeller Foundation, and Wellcome announced two new integrated initiatives to protect South Asians from extreme heat – a rapidly escalating threat to human health and economic stability in the subcontinent. “Few regions feel the impacts of extreme heat as sharply as South Asia, and I welcome the clear determination to respond. We all know that every death primarily due to excess heat can be prevented and heat health action plans are saving lives,” said WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo. “By uniting science, government leadership and support, and community action, countries here are proving that this challenge can be met.” The two complementary initiatives are funded by The Rockefeller Foundation and Wellcome. The South Asia Climate–Health Desk , established as part of the WHO–WMO Climate and Health Joint Programme and implemented with the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology (IITM), India Meteorological Department (IMD), and other partners will improve how climate and weather information is translated into action to protect health. It is one of the first units under the Joint Programme to embrace research and development and operational domains in climate and health and it will develop more robust decision support tools such as early warning and risk assessments. The South Asia Scientific Research Consortium , supported through a Rockefeller Foundation grant to the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research (IISER) Pune, will deepen the region’s scientific understanding of how heat affects different populations. By developing tailored heat‑risk thresholds, this consortium aims to ultimately strengthen heat action planning, early warning systems, and preparedness efforts, helping communities and institutions better adapt to rising temperatures. These projects are the first two components of a broader, more ambitious regional strategy to address extreme heat risks to health. As part of a growing suite of Joint Programme initiatives, including regional activities of the Global Heat Health Information Network, these are first steps of coordinated science-driven efforts to protect communities. UN Secretary-General António Guterres has called for urgent global action to address the growing risk of extreme heat worldwide, which takes a heavy toll on health in South Asia – the world’s most populated region. According to WMO, Asia is warming nearly twice as fast as the global average, intensifying extreme weather and placing growing pressure on lives and livelihoods, health systems, economies, and ecosystems across the region, putting the most vulnerable and exposed communities at critical risk. In India and Pakistan, pre-monsoon temperatures regularly rise above 50°C, and heat-related mortality in the region today exceeds 200,000 deaths per year. At the same time, extreme heat undermines economic stability and productivity. In 2024 alone , heat exposure in India led to 247 billion potential labor hours lost – reducing labor capacity and leading to an estimated $194 billion loss in income, according to the Lancet Countdown. “Extreme heat is a growing risk for lives and livelihoods in South Asia,” said Mrutyunjay Mohapatra, IMD’s Director General of Meteorology and Permanent Representative of India to WMO. “IMD welcomes this partnership with IITM under the South Asia Climate-Health Desk, which will strengthen the science-to-services pathway, improve early warning support for health, and help decision-makers act in time to protect communities during severe heat events.” Transdisciplinary action Addressing extreme heat requires coordinated, transdisciplinary action. This integrated effort equips governments, public services, communities, and health systems with the actionable knowledge they need to prevent avoidable illness and save lives. This announcement is the first in a series of rollouts planned in 2026, highlighting work being carried out in the region. The Rockefeller Foundation and Wellcome’s US $11.5 million investment in the WHO-WMO Climate and Health Joint Programme aims to expand climate‑informed health action in vulnerable regions. The two philanthropies committed the funds to pioneer new models of science-driven collaboration between health partners and meteorological departments, aiming to bridge a gap that often leaves health systems without critical climate information that can protect communities and save lives. “After a decade of punishing and increasingly deadly heatwaves across India and the wider South Asia region, it’s clear that business‑as‑usual public health approaches are no longer enough. Protecting India’s most vulnerable communities requires rethinking how we deliver care and invest in the solutions frontline providers and patients urgently need today,” said Dr. Naveen Rao, Senior Vice President of Health at The Rockefeller Foundation. “Through our support to the Joint Programme, we aim to help turn cutting‑edge science into real‑world impact, helping India and the region build a resilient, climate‑ready health system fit for the 21st century.” "Rising temperatures due to climate change are a public health threat, endangering people's lives and livelihoods throughout the world. In South Asia, extreme heat is hitting communities hard - in particular children, pregnant people, older people, outdoor workers and those communities with the least resources to respond,” said Dr. Alan Dangour, Director of Climate and Health at Wellcome. “We need to invest in science-led solutions that both cut emissions and build resilience, with public health at the core of decision-making. Wellcome is proud to work with partners and communities across South Asia to develop the evidence, tools and solutions that will ultimately improve health and save lives." Through the establishment of these initiatives, South Asia is leading the way in implementing this integrated climate and health approach that connects research, climate monitoring and forecasting, and health responses to protect people from the health risks of climate variability and change. around: Four South Asian neighbours set to tackle rising heat risk together - Newsy Today Skip to content Newsy Today Menu Menu Business Entertainment Health News Sport Tech World Four South Asian neighbours set to tackle rising heat risk together October 26, 2026 by Chief Editor South Asia’s Regional Heat Cooperation Framework South Asian nations India, Nepal, Bangladesh, and Bhutan have formalized a regional coalition to address rising heat risks, as an unprecedented El Niño event increases the likelihood of another severe heat season. The initiative, launched in October 2026, aims to strengthen health surveillance, funding, and local preparedness, according to a media release from the Global Heat Forum. National responses were previously fragmented, but the region now shares a unified evidence base, with assessments highlighting critical gaps in translating heat forecasts into on-the-ground protection.
